ceb.title: Mary as Mediatrix
ceb.question: Doesn't calling Mary 'Mediatrix' contradict 1 Timothy 2:5, that there is one mediator between God and man?
ceb.answer: Christ is the one mediator by nature, the sole bridge between God and humanity through his cross, and the Church affirms this without reservation. Yet the very same chapter that declares one mediator (1 Tim 2:5) opens by urging that intercessions be made for all people (1 Tim 2:1), showing that subordinate, participated mediation does not rival Christ's unique mediation but flows from it. Just as Christians are called to intercede for one another, Mary's role as Mediatrix means she cooperates in and distributes the graces won solely by her Son, never as a competing source. Her mediation is like the moon reflecting the sun: it has no light of its own. At Cana she interceded and Jesus acted through her request (Jn 2:3-5), a model of her maternal mediation. All her power is entirely dependent on and directed toward Christ.

en.answer_full:
> "For there is one God. There is also one mediator between God and the human race, Christ Jesus, himself human, who gave himself as ransom for all."
> — 1 Timothy 2:5 (NABRE)

The title *Mediatrix of All Graces* is both the most controversial and the most misunderstood Marian title in Catholic theology. Critics hear in it a claim that Mary stands between Christians and Christ, replacing or competing with his unique mediation. The actual doctrine is far more carefully defined: Mary's mediation is entirely subordinate to, derived from, and ordered to Christ's unique and unrepeatable redemptive mediation. Understanding the difference between these two types of mediation is the key to the entire debate.

---

## Types of Mediation: A Critical Distinction

| Type | Description | Who Exercises It |
|------|-------------|-----------------|
| **Redemptive Mediation** | Atoning for sin, meriting grace, reconciling humanity to God | Christ alone |
| **Intercessory Mediation** | Praying and interceding for others so that Christ's grace reaches them | All Christians (1 Timothy 2:1); Mary in an exalted degree |
| **Mary's Mediation** | Subordinate, cooperative, derived — presenting the needs of the faithful to her Son | Mary, as Mother of God and of all believers |

Paul commands that *"supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be offered for everyone"* (1 Timothy 2:1) — immediately before his statement that *"there is one mediator"* (1 Timothy 2:5). The juxtaposition is not a contradiction: intercessory prayer does not compete with Christ's unique mediation. When Paul asks the Romans to *"join me in the struggle by your prayers to God on my behalf"* (Romans 15:30), he is not replacing Christ's mediation with human prayer — he is inviting participation in the flow of Christ's grace through human intercession. Mary's intercession is the same in kind, uniquely exalted in degree.

---

## Biblical Foundation

### The Annunciation — Cooperation in the Source of Grace

*"Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord. May it be done to me according to your word."* (Luke 1:38, NABRE)

St. Bernard of Clairvaux drew the principle: *"God could have given us the Redeemer without the Virgin's consent — but he did not will to do so without her free cooperation."* If God arranged the Incarnation — source of all grace — to depend on Mary's free *fiat*, the theological inference that she continues to cooperate in the distribution of grace is not arbitrary. What she began by consent at the Annunciation she continues by intercession from heaven.

### The Wedding at Cana — Intercession in Action

*"They have no wine... Whatever he tells you, do it."* (John 2:3, 5, NABRE)

Cana is the New Testament paradigm of Marian mediation: Mary identifies a human need, presents it to Christ without commanding him, and he acts. Her instruction to the servants — *"Whatever he tells you, do it"* — is the perfect expression of subordinate mediation: she directs all attention and obedience to her Son. Her intercession does not bypass Christ; it is specifically directed *toward* him.

### The Foot of the Cross — Cooperation in the Passion

*"Standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary of Magdala."* (John 19:25, NABRE)

Mary's presence at Calvary is the fulfillment of Simeon's prophecy (*"a sword will pierce your own soul too"* — Luke 2:35). Her compassion (*com-passio* — suffering with) at the Passion is understood by the Fathers and the tradition as her unique cooperation in the redemptive act. She did not merit grace alongside Christ — she united her suffering to his sacrifice in a unique way, so that where he was active as Redeemer, she was receptively cooperative as the first of the redeemed and the mother of the dying Redeemer.

### John 19:27 — Mother of All Disciples

*"Then he said to the disciple, 'Behold, your mother.'"* (John 19:27, NABRE)

In entrusting John to Mary's care (*"Behold, your son"*) and Mary to John's (*"Behold, your mother"*), Jesus gives Mary a maternal relationship to all disciples. John represents the Church — and every member of the Church receives Mary as mother from the dying Christ himself. A mother who intercedes for her children is not circumventing their access to the Father — she is exercising her maternal office.

---

## The New Eve Typology

As Mary's unique cooperation begins with the reversal of Eve's disobedience (Irenaeus's *New Eve* typology), her continued intercessory role mirrors Eve's role as *"mother of all the living"* (Genesis 3:20) — now as spiritual mother of all the redeemed. The first Eve brought death through disobedience; the New Eve brings grace through obedience and intercession.

---

## *Lumen Gentium* Chapter VIII: Careful Formulation

The Second Vatican Council (1964) addressed Mary's role with great care in *Lumen Gentium*, avoiding both maximalist claims and minimalist reductions:

> *"Taken up to heaven she did not lay aside this saving office but by her manifold intercession continues to bring us the gifts of eternal salvation... Therefore the Blessed Virgin is invoked in the Church under the titles of Advocate, Helper, Benefactress, and Mediatrix. This, however, is so understood that it neither takes away anything from nor adds anything to the dignity and efficacy of Christ the one Mediator."*
> — *Lumen Gentium*, 62 (1964)

The Council uses the title *Mediatrix* while explicitly subordinating it to Christ's unique mediation — the precise balance that the theological tradition had always maintained.

---

## Church Fathers and Theologians

> "Having received this joyful message, she conceived and brought forth for us him who is the Author of our salvation... O blessed one, through you grace is given to the world."
> — St. Ephrem the Syrian, *Hymns on the Nativity*, 16 (c. AD 360)

> "It is God's will that we should have nothing without Mary's cooperation."
> — St. Bernard of Clairvaux, *Sermo in Nativitate B.V.M.*, 6 (c. AD 1150)

> "Mary has been made the dispensatrix of graces, and through her intercession they are poured out on all."
> — St. Thomas Aquinas, *Expositio Salutationis Angelicae* (c. AD 1273)

---

## CCC References

| Reference | Teaching |
|-----------|----------|
| CCC 969 | Mary's unique cooperation makes her the Mediatrix in a subordinate sense |
| CCC 970 | Mary's role does not obscure Christ's unique mediation but shows its power |
| CCC 2677 | Mary's intercession as mother of all Christians is part of the Church's prayer |

---

## Common Objections

**"1 Timothy 2:5 says there is ONE mediator — adding Mary is heresy."**

Read 1 Timothy 2:1–5 in context: Paul calls for intercessory prayer for all people in verse 1, then says there is one mediator in verse 5. These are not contradictory statements — they describe different kinds of mediation. The one redemptive mediator (Christ) works through the Church's intercessory prayer (including Mary's). That Paul asks others to intercede for him (Romans 15:30, Colossians 4:3) demonstrates that creaturely intercession does not compete with Christ's unique mediation.

**"We should pray directly to God — why involve Mary?"**

Catholics do pray directly to God — every Mass is directed to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Marian intercession is not an alternative to prayer but an addition to it: just as you might ask a friend or your mother to pray for you, Catholics ask Mary to intercede. The question is not whether we can access God directly (we can) but whether the prayers of others can help us access him more richly (they can — see James 5:16: *"The fervent prayer of a righteous person is very powerful"*). Mary, as the most righteous of all human beings, has the most powerful intercessory prayer.

**"Calling Mary 'Mediatrix of All Graces' makes her equal to Christ."**

The doctrine explicitly states the opposite: Mary's mediation is entirely derived from Christ's, subordinate to his, and effective only through him. She is mediatrix because he is mediator — his mediation is the source and norm of hers. The richness of his mediation is not diminished but expressed in the fact that it works through the loving intercession of the mother he gave to us from the cross.

---

Mary as Mediatrix is not a threat to the Gospel — she is an expression of its depth. The one mediator who gave himself as *"ransom for all"* (1 Timothy 2:6) has, in giving Mary to be mother of all his disciples, arranged that his grace reaches us through the intercession of the woman who first received it — who bore him, who stood beneath his cross, and who now prays for us from the place where she is already fully redeemed, body and soul, in the glory of her Son.
